tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (timlrx/graph-benchmarks, MIT, profiling scripts code/igraph_profile.py, code/networkx_profile.py, code/snap_profile.py, run_profiler.sh) with a public median-time table (runtime_results.png) that matches every number in the record; hardware is only 'n1-standard-16, 16 vCPU Haswell 2.3 GHz' with no CPU model and the libraries are conda-forge/pip binaries with no compiler or flags, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Median seconds, igraph vs NetworkX (Amazon / Google / Pokec), from runtime_results.png: PageRank 0.57 / 2.42 / 23.39 vs 8.59 / 33.5 / 239.75 (about 15x / 14x / 10x, derived from page data); k-core 0.15 / 0.92 / 5.99 vs 3.63 / 42.6 / 296.26 (about 24x / 46x / 49x, derived); strongly connected components 0.22 / 1.38 / 3.96 vs 2.22 / 7.77 / 61.74 (about 10x / 5.6x / 16x, derived); loading 0.57 / 3.87 / 25.75 vs 4.72 / 19.24 / 140.19 (about 8x / 5x / 5x, derived); shortest path 0.05 / 0.41 vs 1.37 / 3.41 on Amazon / Google (about 27x / 8x, derived). The Pokec shortest-path row (igraph 0.6 s vs NetworkX 5.65 s, SNAP 2.3 s) is not like-for-like: the igraph and SNAP scripts start from vertex 0 while the NetworkX script switches to node '1' for Pokec. Versus SNAP: loading 25.75 vs 52.73 s on Pokec (about 2x, derived); SNAP is faster on PageRank.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are third-party (timlrx/graph-benchmarks, MIT, 85 stars, 2020) and appear only in the README image runtime_results.png; the linked timlrx.com blog post is egress-blocked here. The win is against pure-Python NetworkX, not a C or C++ library. In the same table igraph is slower than graph-tool, LightGraphs (Julia) and NetworKit on nearly every algorithm (Google PageRank 2.42 s vs 0.36 / 0.06 / 0.10 s; Pokec PageRank 23.39 s vs 1.1 / 0.21 / 0.24 s) and slower than SNAP on PageRank (Google 2.42 vs 2.31 s, Pokec 23.39 vs 8.62 s) and on Google shortest path (0.41 vs 0.26 s); only loading is faster than graph-tool and LightGraphs. Harness flaw on Pokec shortest path: networkx_profile.py starts at node '1' for Pokec (soc-pokec ids are not 0-based; download_data.sh only strips comment lines, no remapping), but igraph_profile.py runs g.shortest_paths([g.vs[0]]) and Graph.Read(format='edges') creates vertices 0..max id, so igraph's 0.6 s is a search from an isolated phantom vertex plus building a 1.6M-entry distance row, not a real traversal; snap_profile.py also asks for node 0. The Pokec shortest-path ratios (about 9x vs NetworkX, 0.6 vs 2.3 s vs SNAP) should not be cited. igraph returns a full 1 x N distance list while NetworkX returns a dict of reachable nodes. Versions are from 2020 (python-igraph 0.8.2 from conda-forge, networkx 2.4, SNAP 5.0.0 on Python 3.7); igraph has changed since. NetworkX loading uses read_edgelist into a DiGraph. Compiler, flags and exact CPU model are not stated, hence tier B not A. Medians over 100 runs (Amazon, Google) or 10 runs (Pokec); NetworkX was run fewer times (count not stated). The category graph-algorithms is a suggestion: the guessed sequence-containers does not fit.

notes: All table numbers re-checked against runtime_results.png and the profiling scripts; metadata confirmed (2.0k stars, GPL-2.0 file with 'or any later version' source headers, last commit 2026-10-01, not archived). Shortcoming to record: Pokec shortest-path row starts igraph and SNAP at a vertex 0 absent from the dataset while NetworkX starts at node 1, so that row is invalid; the rest of the comparison stands, and igraph trails graph-tool, NetworKit and LightGraphs.

tier_reason: First-party one-sentence claim in lang/struct_pb_intro.md ('序列化速度是protobuf的2.4倍，反序列化是protobuf的3.4倍') with no hardware, compiler or protobuf version; the in-repo benchmark/pb_benchmark.cpp (bench3, monster) is public but no results are committed, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the claim. In-repo CMakeLists.txt: default build type Release with CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE '-O3' plus '-Wall -pthread -g' (no -DNDEBUG), C++17 by default, libstdc++ unless LINKLIBC++; protobuf is whatever find_package(Protobuf) finds.
corrections.caveats: First-party claim in a Chinese-language doc; the numbers carry no hardware, compiler version or protobuf version, and the doc points to 'the benchmark in struct_pack' (alibaba/yalantinglibs) for reproduction. The identical 2.4x / 3.4x sentence is in yalantinglibs' struct_pb docs (website/docs/zh and en/struct_pb/struct_pb_intro.md), where struct_pb is iguana re-exported (include/ylt/struct_pb/struct_pb_impl.hpp: 'namespace struct_pb = iguana;'); yalantinglibs' published struct_pack charts (Alibaba Clang 13, Xeon Platinum 8163) cover struct_pack, not struct_pb. The in-repo benchmark/pb_benchmark.cpp prints iguana/protobuf ratios from a high_resolution_clock around whole loops (default 100000 iterations) but commits no results; deserialization allocates a fresh object per iteration for both libraries, and the parsed objects are never used, so the header-only from_pb could be partly optimised away while protobuf's out-of-line ParseFromString cannot (a risk, not demonstrated). The claim may predate the current code, which was refactored heavily (C++26 reflection; a draft JSON DOM parser PR #386 is still open). The README FAQ answer 'Is iguana high performance? Yes, because it is based on compile-time reflection' has no numbers. No JSON-versus-RapidJSON or other numbers found in README or docs. The claim is about the protobuf binary wire format, so binary-schemas fits better than serialization-json.

notes: Claim text confirmed verbatim; metadata confirmed (1.3k stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-08-12, not a fork). Not a duplicate: yalantinglibs (wave 4, struct_pack entry) vendors iguana and re-exports it as struct_pb, but the listed claim is struct_pack's; consider a category override to binary-schemas. Shortcomings: first-party, no methodology, no committed results, unused parse results in the benchmark loop.

tier_reason: The ICU project's own collation charts (first-party) compare ICU4C against glibc, but icu.unicode.org is egress-blocked, so the page was not opened and the record's percentages remain snippet-only; the only independent number found (thebuild.com, PostgreSQL 17.1) is also snippet-only from a blocked blog, so the tier stays C. The benchmark program collperf.cpp is public but no CPU, compiler or flags were readable.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SNIPPET ONLY, not re-confirmed: the record's en_US (Latin data) figures of strcoll 199%, keygen 77%, keylen 99% in ICU4C's favour and ja_JP strcoll 421% (chart convention: positive favours ICU4C; values are chart deltas, not ratios) came from WebSearch text; this verifier's snippets confirm only that the ICU4C 4.8 vs glibc 2.13-1 chart shows ICU4C 'significantly better' on en_US strcoll. Independent (snippet only, thebuild.com 'Talk fast: the speed of various collations', PostgreSQL 17.1 on Ubuntu 24.04, 4 GB Linode, 1,000,000 rows of 64 random 7-bit ASCII characters, SELECT * ORDER BY): ICU de-AT 770 ms vs libc de_AT 3645 ms (about 4.7x, derived from snippet data); ICU und-x-icu 765 ms; byte-order collations builtin C.UTF8 486 ms and libc POSIX 470 ms beat ICU.
corrections.caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: icu.unicode.org (both https://icu.unicode.org/charts/collation-icu4c-glibc and the ICU4C 4.8 chart at https://icu.unicode.org/charts/collation-icu4c48-glibc), thebuild.com, the PostgreSQL mailing list and lists.gnupg.org were not opened (egress-blocked), so all numbers come from WebSearch result text; the exact percentages could not be re-confirmed and the chart's platform, CPU and compiler fields were not readable. Chart percentages are deltas, not ratios. Charts are old: ICU4C 3.8 versus glibc 2.12.3 and ICU4C 4.8 versus glibc 2.13 (about 2008 to 2011); both libraries have changed since. The chart page reportedly warns results vary with hardware and compiler and that strcoll is sensitive to code alignment (10% swings). The benchmark code is public (icu4c/source/test/perf/collationperf/collperf.cpp, which times ICU ucol_strcoll/sort keys against Unix strcoll/strxfrm with a -unix flag) but no committed results were found. The independent PostgreSQL measurement (thebuild.com, 2024) uses random ASCII strings rather than natural text and is confounded by PostgreSQL itself: abbreviated sort keys are used for ICU collations but disabled for libc collations, so part of the 4.7x is PostgreSQL's sort path, not raw strcoll speed. A second snippet-only claim: a PostgreSQL mailing-list message reports ICU normalization at 0.861 s and 0.651 s against PostgreSQL's built-in 4.024 s and 6.655 s on two conversions (hardware and method unknown). The guessed baseline 'standard UTF-8 processing' does not match any evidence; this is a collation and normalization claim. ICU is also the incumbent that other Unicode libraries benchmark against.

notes: Metadata confirmed (3.6k stars, LICENSE is Unicode License V3 = Unicode-3.0, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived); not a duplicate (wave 10 lists unicode-org/icu4x, a different project). Shortcomings: first-party 2008-2011 charts readable only through search snippets; the one independent number is snippet-only and confounded by PostgreSQL's abbreviated-key policy; ICU's byte-order rivals (C.UTF8, POSIX) are faster.
